questions.stem: A client admitted with major depression has been sitting alone in the dayroom. When the nurse sits nearby, the client says quietly, "I'm worthless. Nobody would even notice if I was gone." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.text: "Are you having thoughts of ending your life?"
"You feel that you have no value to anyone right now?"
"Your family visited yesterday, so I know they would notice."
"Why do you feel worthless when you have so much going for you?"

rationale.correct: Statements such as "nobody would notice if I was gone" are suicide cues; ask directly about suicidal thoughts.

perOption.a: The statement hints at suicide; asking directly assesses safety and does not plant the idea.
perOption.b: Reflecting is therapeutic, but the hint of suicide must be assessed directly first.
perOption.c: This argues with the feeling and misses the safety cue.
perOption.d: 'Why' questions feel judgmental and this one minimizes the feeling.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nursing student is talking with a client who is anxious about a new diagnosis of breast cancer. The nurse is evaluating the student's communication. Which statement by the student is a nontherapeutic technique?

options.text: "Tell me more about what the doctor said."
"Don't worry. They caught it early, so you'll be fine."
"You seem worried since you came back from the clinic."
"What has been the hardest part of today?"

rationale.correct: Avoid false reassurance, advice-giving, 'why' questions, changing the subject and judgment.

perOption.a: This is an open-ended prompt.
perOption.b: False reassurance blocks discussion of feelings.
perOption.c: Making an observation is therapeutic.
perOption.d: This encourages description.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During the third one-to-one session on an inpatient psychiatric unit, a client smiles and asks the nurse, "Are you married? Do you have kids? Where do you live?" What is the best response?

options.text: "Our time is for you. How has your day been?"
"I'm married with two kids, and I live in the next town over."
"That's personal, and I'm not going to answer that."
Pause, say nothing and wait for the client to change topics

rationale.correct: Keep the therapeutic relationship focused on the client.

perOption.a: This redirects to the client and keeps professional boundaries without rejecting the client.
perOption.b: Personal details shift the focus to the nurse and blur boundaries.
perOption.c: This is abrupt and damages rapport.
perOption.d: Ignoring the question is not therapeutic.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old admitted after an overdose says to the nurse, "I'll tell you something really important, but only if you promise not to tell my parents or anyone else." What is the best response?

options.text: "I can't promise that; I must share anything that affects your safety."
"I promise I won't tell your parents, so you can trust me with it."
"If you don't want it shared, it's better not to tell me at all."
"I'll keep it from your parents, but I'll tell your doctor."

rationale.correct: Information that affects safety must be shared with the treatment team; say so before the client discloses.

perOption.a: Nurses cannot keep secrets that involve safety, such as suicidal plans or abuse; saying so up front keeps trust.
perOption.b: The nurse may have to break this promise.
perOption.c: This shuts down communication about possible danger.
perOption.d: The nurse cannot promise what will be shared before hearing it.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a request for secrecy.

questions.stem: A client in the emergency department is breathing rapidly, trembling and clutching the chest, saying, "I'm going to die." The ECG and troponin were normal 1 hour ago, and the SpO2 is 99%. The client has had two similar episodes this month. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stay with the client and give short, calm directions
Explain that the tests were normal and the heart is not affected
Have the client breathe into a paper bag to slow the breathing
Leave the client in a quiet room to calm down alone

rationale.correct: Severe or panic anxiety: stay, stay calm, simple directions, reduce stimulation.

perOption.a: In panic, the client cannot process complex information; a calm presence lowers anxiety.
perOption.b: Detailed explanations cannot be processed during panic.
perOption.c: Paper bag rebreathing is not recommended and can cause hypoxia.
perOption.d: A client in panic should not be left alone.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with generalized anxiety disorder who works as a forklift driver is starting buspirone 7.5 mg twice daily. The client used to take lorazepam as needed. Which statement shows correct understanding?

options.text: "It may take a few weeks before I notice a difference."
"I'll take a dose whenever I start to feel anxious at work."
"It will make me sleepy, so I'll stop driving the forklift."
"I'll need to taper off slowly to avoid getting hooked."

rationale.correct: Buspirone: scheduled dosing, delayed effect, little sedation or dependence.

perOption.a: Buspirone's effects build over 2 to 4 weeks.
perOption.b: Buspirone is taken on a schedule, not as needed.
perOption.c: It is minimally sedating, though effects should be checked.
perOption.d: It has low dependence potential.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client has taken lorazepam 1 mg three times daily for 6 weeks after a traumatic event and is starting therapy. The nurse reviews teaching about the medicine. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I won't have wine with dinner while I'm on this."
"Once I feel better, I'll just stop taking it."
"I won't drive until I know how it affects me."
"My provider will lower the dose slowly over weeks."

rationale.correct: Benzodiazepines: avoid alcohol, taper off, watch for sedation and dependence.

perOption.a: Alcohol adds to CNS depression.
perOption.b: Stopping suddenly after regular use can cause withdrawal and seizures.
perOption.c: It causes drowsiness.
perOption.d: Tapering is correct.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client admitted yesterday with obsessive-compulsive disorder washes the hands for 30 minutes before every meal and arrives after the dining room closes. The hands are red and cracked. Staff ask how to handle mealtimes. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Wake the client early so the ritual can be done before meals
Lock the bathroom before meals so the client cannot wash
Hold the meal tray until the client can arrive at the dining room on time
Explain that the hands are clean and washing is not needed

rationale.correct: OCD: early on, allow time for rituals and protect the skin, then gradually limit them while teaching coping skills.

perOption.a: Interrupting rituals early raises anxiety; allow time now and limit gradually later.
perOption.b: Blocking the ritual abruptly sharply increases anxiety.
perOption.c: This is punitive and risks poor nutrition.
perOption.d: The client knows the ritual is excessive; logic does not reduce the anxiety.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old veteran returned from deployment 6 months ago. The client startles at loud noises, has nightmares about a roadside explosion, avoids driving on highways and says, "I feel numb around my family." Which disorder do these findings suggest?

options.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder
Generalized anxiety disorder
Acute stress disorder
Major depressive disorder

rationale.correct: PTSD: intrusive memories, avoidance, negative mood and hyperarousal for more than 1 month; use trauma-informed care.

perOption.a: Hyperarousal, re-experiencing, avoidance and numbing after trauma are typical of PTSD.
perOption.b: GAD is broad worry that is not tied to a trauma.
perOption.c: This lasts up to 1 month after the trauma.
perOption.d: Numbness can occur, but the trauma-linked symptoms point to PTSD.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing notes from group therapy. For each statement, indicate the defense mechanism it shows.

rows.text: A client newly diagnosed with diabetes keeps eating sweets and says, "The lab must have mixed up my blood."
A client who is angry at being admitted says to the nurse, "You're the one who's angry with me."
After being criticized by the unit manager, a client slams a door and shouts at a roommate
A client who was fired for being late says, "That job was going nowhere anyway."

rationale.correct: Recognize common defense mechanisms in client statements.

perOption.r1:c1: Refusing to accept reality is denial.
perOption.r1:c2: No feelings are attributed to others.
perOption.r1:c4: No excuse is offered for a behavior.
perOption.r2:c2: The client attributes their own feelings to the nurse.
perOption.r2:c3: The feeling is not shifted to a safer target.
perOption.r3:c3: Anger is shifted to a safer target.
perOption.r4:c4: A plausible excuse is given for the loss.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client comes to the crisis center the day after losing a job and being evicted. The client is tearful, has not eaten since yesterday and says, "I don't know where to go. I don't see the point anymore." What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Whether the client has thoughts of suicide
Where the client can sleep tonight
What helped the client cope with past losses
When the client last ate and drank

rationale.correct: Crisis intervention: ensure safety, focus on the immediate problem, use coping strategies and supports.

perOption.a: "I don't see the point" is a suicide cue; safety is the first priority in crisis.
perOption.b: Shelter matters, but safety from self-harm comes first.
perOption.c: Past coping is assessed after safety.
perOption.d: Nutrition is a need, but not the most urgent.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with metastatic pancreatic cancer tells the hospice nurse, "If I can just live until my daughter's wedding in June, I'll be ready to go." Which stage of grief does this reflect?

options.text: Bargaining
Denial
Acceptance
Depression

rationale.correct: Kübler-Ross stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance (not always in order).

perOption.a: Bargaining is trying to make a deal for more time.
perOption.b: The client acknowledges the illness and death.
perOption.c: The client is still negotiating for time.
perOption.d: No sadness or withdrawal is described.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two weeks after the sudden death of a spouse, a client cries often, has trouble sleeping and sometimes thinks they hear the spouse's voice in the house. The client eats regular meals and plans to go back to work next week. How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: A normal grief response
Major depressive disorder
Prolonged grief disorder
A psychotic disorder

rationale.correct: Support normal grief; watch for prolonged, disabling grief or suicidal thoughts.

perOption.a: Sadness, sleep changes and briefly sensing the dead person are common early in grief.
perOption.b: It is too early to label this, and the client is functioning.
perOption.c: This is diagnosed when grief lasts 12 months or more and is disabling.
perOption.d: Briefly hearing a dead loved one's voice is a common part of grief.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client of Hmong heritage admitted with pneumonia asks for a shaman to perform a healing ceremony at the bedside in addition to IV antibiotics. The ceremony includes chanting and tying strings around the wrist. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: Arrange a time for the ceremony and plan around the IV site
Explain that hospital policy does not permit healing ceremonies
Ask the client to choose between the ceremony and the antibiotics
Allow the ceremony but remove the strings when the shift ends

rationale.correct: Culturally responsive care includes safe traditional practices.

perOption.a: Respecting cultural practices supports trust and adherence when they do not interfere with treatment.
perOption.b: This disregards cultural values without a safety reason.
perOption.c: Both can be safely combined.
perOption.d: Removing the strings disrespects the practice.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client hospitalized for 3 weeks with complications after surgery tells the nurse, "I've prayed every day, and I feel like God has abandoned me." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Listen, explore the feeling and offer a chaplain visit
Change the subject to the plan for discharge home
Share the nurse's own beliefs about faith and suffering
Reassure the client that God has not abandoned anyone

rationale.correct: Assess spiritual needs and refer according to the client's wishes.

perOption.a: This addresses spiritual distress respectfully and follows the client's wishes.
perOption.b: This dismisses the client's distress.
perOption.c: This imposes the nurse's views.
perOption.d: This argues with the client's experience.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client who witnessed a serious car crash yesterday suddenly cannot move the right arm. A CT scan, an MRI and nerve studies are normal. The client seems calm, eats with the left hand and says, "I'm sure it will come back." Which condition do these findings suggest?

options.text: Conversion disorder linked to stress
Acute ischemic stroke
Malingering for financial gain
Illness anxiety disorder

rationale.correct: Conversion disorder: real symptoms without an organic cause, linked to stress; avoid focusing on the symptom.

perOption.a: Neurologic symptoms without an organic cause, after stress and with apparent indifference, suggest conversion.
perOption.b: The imaging and nerve studies are normal.
perOption.c: In conversion, symptoms are not produced on purpose.
perOption.d: Clients with this disorder are very worried, not calm.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old was bitten by a dog as a child and now avoids walking in the neighborhood and visiting friends who own dogs. The client wants to be able to walk to work. Which treatment is most effective?

options.text: Gradual exposure to dogs paired with relaxation
Avoiding dogs by changing the route to work
Spending an hour in a room with several dogs
Daily alprazolam before leaving the house

rationale.correct: Phobias respond to exposure-based behavioral therapy.

perOption.a: Systematic desensitization reduces fear step by step.
perOption.b: Avoidance keeps the fear going.
perOption.c: Flooding without preparation and consent is not the first choice.
perOption.d: Benzodiazepines are not first-line treatment for phobias.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During a private screening at a prenatal visit, a client says the partner hit them last night and has threatened to "finish it" if they leave. The partner is in the waiting room. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess immediate safety and begin a safety plan
Tell the client to leave the partner and go to a shelter today
Ask the partner to come in and talk about the problem together
Document the disclosure and give the client a hotline number

rationale.correct: IPV: screen privately, believe the client, assess safety, create a safety plan and give resources.

perOption.a: Safety comes first, and the client decides on next steps; a threat to kill raises the risk.
perOption.b: Leaving can be the most dangerous time; the client decides.
perOption.c: This raises the danger to the client.
perOption.d: Resources help, but a safety assessment and plan come first.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to disclosure of intimate partner violence.

questions.stem: A client says that after each beating, the partner cries, apologizes, brings flowers and promises it will never happen again. The client says, "This time I think they really mean it." Which phase of the cycle of violence is the client describing?

options.text: Reconciliation (honeymoon) phase
Tension-building phase
Acute battering phase
Recovery and separation phase

rationale.correct: Cycle of violence: tension building, then acute battering, then honeymoon, then repeat.

perOption.a: Remorse and affection follow the battering.
perOption.b: This involves rising stress and minor incidents.
perOption.c: This is the violent episode.
perOption.d: This is not a phase of the cycle.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client calls the emergency department 1 hour after being sexually assaulted. The client is crying and says, "I just want to wash it all off and go to bed." Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Please don't shower or change before coming in."
"Take a shower first if it helps you feel calmer."
"Put your clothes in the washer, then come in."
"Rest tonight and come in first thing in the morning."

rationale.correct: Sexual assault: preserve evidence, give prompt care (ideally a SANE exam) and offer support and prophylaxis.

perOption.a: This preserves evidence for the forensic exam.
perOption.b: Showering destroys evidence.
perOption.c: Clothing holds evidence and should be brought in a paper bag.
perOption.d: Prompt care is needed for evidence and prophylaxis.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old resident of a long-term care facility says to the nurse, "My son never visits me anymore. I guess I'm just a burden now." Select the 2 most therapeutic responses.

options.text: "You're feeling hurt that your son doesn't visit?"
"Tell me more about you and your son."
"I'm sure he's just very busy with work these days."
"Why don't you give him a call this afternoon?"
"My mother used to say the same thing to me."

rationale.correct: Reflection and open-ended questions encourage clients to share feelings.

perOption.a: Reflecting the feeling is therapeutic.
perOption.b: An open-ended prompt encourages expression.
perOption.c: This is false reassurance and minimizes the feeling.
perOption.d: This gives advice.
perOption.e: This shifts the focus to the nurse.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
